hub.title: Reverse Engineering Starter Guide
hub.intro: Start from the first real tool window and follow highlights attached to the software you are using. You operate the tools yourself; the guide explains what you are seeing and where to look next.
hub.route_text: Identify what the file is, choose the right tool, observe clues, then confirm them in code or at runtime.
hub.update_text: More lessons may appear during the event. Checking updates syncs course files while keeping your local progress.

common.correct: Correct. Before moving on, pause for a second and recall which observation led you to this result.
common.wrong: Keep checking the current tool: re-read the string, branch, or runtime value you saw, then submit the confirmed flag.
common.fake_flag: This looks like a flag near the wrong path. Return to IDA, check references and branches, and submit the candidate tied to the success path.
common.tool_missing: This bundled tool was not found: {tool}. Check that assets/tools is complete in the release package.
common.tool_required: This step needs the real {tool} window. The guide will attach to the tool and point at the next place to inspect: {path}
common.tool_launching: Opening {tool}. When the window appears, the guide will explain what you are seeing and what to do next.
common.tool_activated: {tool} is already running. Switched to its window; continue with the highlighted place.
common.target_required: Sample {file} is located. Next, open its folder window so you can choose the same file inside the real tool. Path: {path}
common.target_folder_opened: Opened the folder window containing {file} and tried to select it. Return to {tool} and choose this same sample in the tool's open-file dialog.
common.target_folder_failed: Could not open the folder for {file}: {error}
common.explorer_target_guide: You are now looking at the sample folder window, and {file} should be selected. This only helps you locate the file; the real analysis still happens inside {tool}.
common.flag_extra_trimmed: Extra pasted text was removed automatically; the flag itself is correct.
common.no_more_guide: Forced guidance ends here. Continue with the same route: identify the file, choose a tool, then confirm the flag through code or runtime behavior.
common.tracked_none: Open the required tool from the left side; the guide will attach when its window appears.
stage0.title: Intro: Meet The File First
stage0.goal: You will complete the first full loop: use DIE to read basic file traits, open the sample in IDA, find a candidate string, then confirm why it is trustworthy through references.
stage0.step.open_die: You are looking at the DIE icon on the course desktop. DIE first tells you what kind of file this is and what platform it targets. Next, click DIE to open the triage tool.
stage0.step.open_in_die: After DIE opens, give it the sample. Clicking the sample icon opens its folder window with d477fcf61542.exe selected; then click DIE's ... button and choose it in the open-file dialog.
stage0.step.read_fields: DIE should now show result lines such as PE64, AMD64, GUI, or C/C++. Treat them as a file checkup: this is a Windows program that you can inspect further with IDA. After reading it, close DIE or move it aside. Next, open IDA.
stage0.step.open_ghidra: If another decompiler name appears, keep this stage on the IDA route. This lesson uses IDA's basic open-and-inspect flow.
stage0.step.open_ida: Now look at the IDA icon on the course desktop. IDA is the code-inspection tool for this step. Click IDA and wait for its Quick start page or open-file window.
stage0.step.ida_quick_start: You are seeing IDA's start page. It asks how you want to begin. Next, click Load a new file / New so IDA can read a program file.
stage0.step.ida_select_sample: You should now see IDA's file picker. The sample name is d477fcf61542.exe. If you cannot find it, click the sample icon in the course to open its folder window. Next, select that sample in IDA's file picker and click Open.
stage0.step.ida_confirm_load: IDA will show a load confirmation dialog, often with Portable executable, processor type, and OK. It is confirming that the file will be loaded as a Windows PE program. Keep the defaults and click OK.
stage0.step.open_strings: After IDA finishes auto-analysis, you will see several panes: a function list on the side and disassembly in the center. First open Strings with View -> Open subviews -> Strings, or press Shift+F12.
stage0.step.search_flag: The Strings window lists text found inside the program. When you see text shaped like flag{...}, treat it as a candidate clue. Select that string, press X or use the context menu for xrefs, and jump to the code that uses it.
stage0.step.string_xrefs: The candidate string is selected. Now inspect where the code uses it so you can judge which execution path it belongs to. Press X, or use the context menu for Jump to xref / cross references.
stage0.step.inspect_reference: You should now be near the code that references this string. Look for nearby output, prompt, or success-path logic; if you have a decompiler, press F5 to view pseudocode. Once it looks intentional rather than stray text, prepare to submit.
stage0.step.submit_flag: You have moved from 'the string exists' to 'the code references it'. Copy the confirmed complete flag into the submit box on the right. Submit only the flag, without extra spaces or explanation.
stage0.deviation.ida_load_modal: You are seeing IDA's load confirmation dialog. Keep the default loading choice, click OK, and wait for auto-analysis before opening Strings.
stage0.deviation.ida_debug_info_modal: IDA found debug information. For the starter flow, click No and keep the load simple.
stage0.deviation.ida_database_exists_mod: IDA found an existing database, which means this sample was analyzed before. Click Load existing to reuse that analysis and save time.
stage0.deviation.ida_database_repair_mod: IDA says the old database needs attention. Click Reload file so the lesson starts from the original sample again.
stage0.deviation.ida_problem_modal: IDA reported a problem dialog. Click OK first; then restart IDA and load the sample again if the code view does not appear.
stage1.title: Stage 1: Strings Are Only Clues
stage1.goal: This stage may show multiple flag-looking strings. Treat them as candidates first, then use references and branches to decide which one is trustworthy.
stage1.hint.explore: Use the same rhythm as before: open the sample in IDA, open Strings, collect candidate strings, then confirm them in code.
stage1.step.open_ida: Open IDA and choose Load a new file / New from the start page. The sample is abb3c03d7a56.exe; if you cannot find it, click the sample icon to open its folder window.
stage1.step.open_strings: After loading and analysis, open Strings. First collect clues: record texts that look like flags, Correct, Wrong, or other branch hints.
stage1.hint.two_flags: If Strings shows multiple flag-looking texts, treat all of them as candidates. Start by checking cross references for one candidate and see which path uses it.
stage1.step.jump_xrefs: Select a candidate string and press X, or use the context menu to view cross references. Jump near the code that uses it, then check how it relates to Correct / Wrong messages.
stage1.step.read_branches: You should now see a branch shape in pseudocode or disassembly, such as if/else, Correct, or Wrong door. First identify the success side, then see which candidate string is referenced near that side.
stage1.step.submit_true: The branch relationship confirms the candidate. Submit the complete flag from the success path.
stage2.title: Stage 2: Identify, Then Switch Tools
stage2.goal: Start with DIE again. When you see .NET / CLR / CLI clues, switch to dnSpy because it is better suited for reading this program's logic.
stage2.step.open_die: Begin with DIE. Clicking the sample icon opens the folder window with 3c68a27e81e2.exe selected; give it to DIE and focus on the file type and runtime/language clues.
stage2.hint.managed_runtime: You are seeing .NET, CLR, CLI, or MSIL. That means this sample is best read in dnSpy, where the logic appears closer to source code. Next, open dnSpy.
stage2.step.open_dnspy: Open dnSpy. Its left side shows an assembly tree, and the right side shows recovered code. Next, load 3c68a27e81e2.exe.
stage2.step.load_dnspy_sample: If dnSpy has not loaded the sample yet, click the sample icon to open its folder window and find 3c68a27e81e2.exe; then choose it in dnSpy with File -> Open.
stage2.step.expand_tree: Now look at dnSpy's left tree. Expand the sample node and look for MainForm, Program, button events, or similar entry points. Tree nodes are program structure, not folders.
stage2.step.find_logic: After opening a suspicious form or button handler, the right side shows C#-like code. Read comparisons, string building, prompt text, and return paths in order to confirm where the flag is produced or kept.
stage2.step.submit_flag: Once the logic is confirmed, paste the complete flag into the submit box. Do not include quotes, semicolons, or surrounding code.
stage3.title: Stage 3: Let The Program Show You
stage3.goal: This stage will not place the full flag directly in strings. Use IDA to find the success text and code location, then use x64dbg to observe memory while the program runs.
stage3.hint.no_plain_flag: Open 033719085d5d.exe in IDA and open Strings. If there is no complete flag but there is a success phrase like FLAG OK, the answer may only appear at runtime.
stage3.step.search_success_text: You can now see a success phrase in Strings or search results. It is not the answer; it is a landmark near code that checks or creates the flag. Next, inspect its cross references.
stage3.step.xref_success_text: Select the success phrase, press X, and jump to the code that references it. Once near the code, look for loops, xor, copies, or writes to memory before the success message.
stage3.step.observe_noise: Nearby code may look noisy: loops, xor 0x5A, and distracting instructions. A beginner does not need every line yet; confirm that some bytes are reconstructed and written to a buffer at runtime.
stage3.step.runtime_marker: Write the important IDA location as 'module base + offset'. It becomes the marker you will use in x64dbg to find the same code and memory.
stage3.step.open_x64dbg: Now switch from static observation to dynamic verification. Open x64dbg so the program can actually run and stop at the important moment.
stage3.step.load_x64dbg_sample: After x64dbg opens, load the sample into it. Click the sample icon to open the folder window and locate 033719085d5d.exe; then choose it in x64dbg with File -> Open.
stage3.deviation.x64dbg_system_break: x64dbg is stopped at the system breakpoint. This is normal and not your program logic. Stay in the CPU view and press F9 to continue.
stage3.deviation.x64dbg_module_break: x64dbg is stopped at a system DLL or module-load breakpoint. It is still not the target logic. Press F9 again until the target window appears or your breakpoint is hit.
stage3.step.find_module_base: Open x64dbg's Memory Map. It lists each module's runtime base. Find the row for 033719085d5d.exe and write down its base address.
stage3.step.goto_offset: Turn the IDA offset into a runtime address: runtime address = module base + offset. Press Ctrl+G to go there, then prepare to set a breakpoint.
stage3.step.run_and_read: With the breakpoint ready, continue the program and trigger the generation logic. The goal is not for the debugger to solve it, but for the program to stop when it writes the important data.
stage3.step.goto_decode: Press Ctrl+G and go to the decode or write location you recorded. You are not looking at the button UI now; you are going to the moment where data is written back to memory.
stage3.step.bp_and_run: When the cursor is near the key code, press F2 to set a breakpoint, then F9 to run. If it breaks there, the program reached the location you predicted in IDA.
stage3.step.click_generate: Switch back to the target program window and click Generate. If the breakpoint is correct, x64dbg will stop again at the location you set.
stage3.step.dump_flag: The program is now stopped in its runtime state. Inspect the buffer or related memory pane that was just written; copy the complete flag only after you see it.
stage3.step.submit_flag: You are now seeing the complete flag generated at runtime. Submit only the flag text itself, without addresses, dump bytes, or explanation.
final.title: Final: Run The Full Workflow Yourself
final.goal: Two new programs are provided. Identify the type first, choose the right tool, then confirm the flag through code or runtime behavior.
final.brief: There are no arrows for every step here, but the route is the same: DIE for identification, IDA or dnSpy for logic, and x64dbg when runtime state matters.
final.cleared: You have completed the starter route. Submit the final flag to the CTF platform; for future tasks, keep the same order: identify, choose tools, collect clues, and verify with code or runtime behavior.
common.drag_hint: This area lists the real tools and practice samples for the stage. Tool icons open tools; sample icons open the folder window and select the file so you can choose it from the tool's open-file dialog.
